title: Lesson 0: how a processor runs a loop
description:
A short guided tour of RVCAT with one example, the loop VectSum:
from the C code to machine instructions, latency, overlapped execution, dependences and performance bounds.

About 20 minutes; optional cards go deeper.

tutorial.name: Lesson 0: how a processor runs a loop

steps.title: Welcome to RVCAT
steps.description:
RVCAT explains why a loop takes the time it takes.

This lesson follows one example and shows the simulator little by little.

• Continue follows the main path; In depth cards explain more.

• The bar above counts the questions and predictions.

• Exit lesson leaves it at any time; it is always in the 📘 Lessons menu.

steps.title: 1. The loop VectSum
steps.description: Click the table header to see the C code (needed to continue).

validation.message: Click the header of the table to see the C code

steps.doneDescription:
The function adds all the N elements of two vectors, V and W.

Time grows with N: T = T0 + T1·N (T0: constant time outside the loop; T1: time per iteration).
VectSum has linear time complexity, Θ(N): doubling N approximately doubles the time.
Complexity does not depend on the processor; the constant T1 does.

Measured on a real processor (Intel Core i5-12400), each loop iteration takes 4 clock cycles.
Where do those 4 cycles come from?
      That is the question of this lesson.

steps.title: In depth: time, cycles and complexity
steps.description:
• The processor works at the rate of a clock: one cycle typically lasts 0.2 to 1 ns (1 to 5 GHz).
   We measure time in cycles: seconds = cycles / frequency.

• Real measurements (Intel Core i5-12400, N = 5000):
        20,020 cycles = 4 cycles per iteration (4.57 microseconds at 4.38 GHz).

steps.title: 2. From C to machine instructions
steps.description:
The compiler translates the C loop into machine instructions,
the simple operations that a given processor (its ISA) executes.
RVCAT shows machine instructions in a readable form, one per row:
• two loads (read V[i] and W[i] from memory),
• two additions of floats (sum = sum + tmp),
• and the loop control (i = i + 1, compare, branch):
      7 instructions per iteration.

The columns Type, Oper and Size describe each instruction: its type (MEM, FLOAT, INT, BRANCH), its operation (LOAD, ADD…) and the size of its data. The execution time of an instruction depends on its type.oper.size.

steps.title: In depth: what the compiler can do
steps.description:
The compiler can transform the code to run faster, and the programmer controls it in two ways:

• (A) enabling or disabling strategies with options (flags) added to the compilation command of gcc
   or another compiler, e.g. gcc -O2 vectsum.c, or -ffast-math, which allows changing
   the order of floating-point additions (it can change the rounding);

• (B) rewriting the source code by hand to make the compiler's task easier.

The versions V1 and V2 that you will see are examples of (B).

steps.title: 3. Machine instructions and ISA
steps.description:
A machine instruction is a simple operation, coded in binary, that the processor executes directly:
read or write a memory location, an arithmetic operation, a comparison, a branch to another instruction.

An Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the specification of the machine instructions that a family of processors
executes: their operations, operands, registers, memory addressing and binary format.
A program compiled for an ISA runs on every processor that implements it, whatever its internal design.

Common ISAs: x86-64 (Intel and AMD: PCs and servers), ARM (AArch64: phones, Apple computers, servers)
and RISC-V (an open and free ISA: embedded systems, research, a growing number of processors).

RVCAT does not model a real ISA: it simulates abstract instructions, similar in all of them.
Optional cards show the machine code (assembly) of the loop of Base in each ISA.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in x86-64
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly, in the UNIX/AT&T syntax) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    # RVCAT rows
        addss   (%rdi,%rax), %xmm0      # 0, 1: tmp = V[i]; sum = sum + tmp
        addss   (%rsi,%rax), %xmm0      # 2, 3: tmp = W[i]; sum = sum + tmp
        addq    $4, %rax                # 4: i = i + 1
        cmpq    %rax, %rdx              # 5: c = i != N
        jne     .L3                     # 6: if c go back

x86-64 can combine a load and an addition in one instruction (an operand in memory): 5 instructions.
Inside, the processor splits them into simple operations (micro-operations), like the 7 rows of RVCAT.

The compiler advances a byte offset instead of the index i: %rax is the position of V[i] and W[i]
in bytes, so it adds 4 (the size of a float) to go to the next element, and %rdx holds 4·N.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in ARM (AArch64)
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (simplified; it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    // RVCAT rows
  ldr    s1, [x0, x3, lsl 2]            // 0: tmp = V[i]
  ldr    s2, [x1, x3, lsl 2]            // 2: tmp = W[i]
  add    x3, x3, 1                      // 4: i = i + 1
  fadd   s0, s0, s1                     // 1: sum = sum + tmp
  cmp    x2, x3                         // 5: c = i != N
  fadd   s0, s0, s2                     // 3: sum = sum + tmp
  bne    .L3                            // 6: if c go back

ARM loads and computes in separate instructions: 7 instructions, one for each row of RVCAT.

steps.title: In depth: the loop of Base in RISC-V
steps.description:
Machine code (assembly) of the loop, compiled with gcc -O2 (simplified; it may change with the compiler version):

.L3:                                    # RVCAT rows
  flw     fa4, 0(a0)                    # 0: tmp = V[i]
  flw     fa5, 0(a1)                    # 2: tmp = W[i]
  addi    a0, a0, 4                     # 4: next element of V
  addi    a1, a1, 4                     #    next element of W
  fadd.s  fa0, fa0, fa4                 # 1: sum = sum + tmp
  fadd.s  fa0, fa0, fa5                 # 3: sum = sum + tmp
  bne     a0, a2, .L3                   # 5, 6: if not at the end, go back

Also 7 instructions, but different: the compiler advances two pointers instead of the index i,
and one branch instruction (bne) compares and jumps.

steps.title: 4. Measure: simulate the loop
steps.description:
Simulate N = 1,000 iterations of the loop on a processor similar to the real one:
click the "Run Simulation" button (or ▶ Show me).
steps.doneDescription:
{{instructions}} instructions in {{cycles}} cycles: {{cyclesPerIter}} cycles per iteration, like the real processor.

IPC = {{ipc}} instructions per cycle: the processor executes almost 2 instructions every cycle.

Key: current processors can execute multiple instructions at the same time (Instruction-Level Parallelism, ILP).

Want to improve performance? Next come two versions of VectSum rewritten by hand: before simulating them, predict their time.

steps.title: In depth: a processor that executes several instructions at once
steps.description:
The program is a sequence of instructions, but the processor does not have to execute them one by one.

A multiple-issue (superscalar) processor starts and finishes several instructions per cycle (this one, up to 4),
has several execution units working in parallel, and keeps many instructions in flight, each one at a different stage.

It finds by itself which instructions are independent and overlaps them; the result is the same as executing them in order.

So IPC can be greater than 1, but only if there are enough independent instructions: the rest of the lesson shows what limits it.

steps.description:

It still has 7 instructions per iteration (look at the table).

steps.title: Predict: version V2
steps.description:
V2 is unrolled: each iteration adds two elements of each vector (i = i + 2),
with 11 instructions instead of 2 × 7 = 14: fewer instructions per element.

steps.title: A paradox?
steps.questionText: Per element: Base runs 7 instructions in 4 cycles, V1 runs 7 instructions in 2 cycles, and V2 runs 5.5 instructions in 4 cycles (the same on the real processor). Which statement is true?

answers.text: The number of instructions alone does not determine the time
answers.explanation: Right: V1 is twice as fast with the same instructions, and V2 is not faster with fewer. We need a model of how the processor executes them.

answers.text: Fewer instructions always run faster
answers.explanation: V2 executes fewer instructions per element than Base, and takes the same time.

answers.text: Changing the order of the additions cannot change the time
answers.explanation: V1 only changes that order, and runs twice as fast.

answers.text: Half the iterations means half the time
answers.explanation: V2 does half the iterations, but each one does twice the work: same time per element.

steps.title: 5. Latency
steps.description:
The processor handles each instruction going through several stages (states): the instruction is fetched from memory, dispatched into the execution engine, executed, its result is written, and finally it is retired.

The number of cycles that an instruction stays in the Execute stage is its latency: in each processor, it depends on the type.oper.size of the instruction, which we saw before.

Click the type button of the Program panel to see the latencies of these instructions in the configured processor.
We will show you how to change them later.
steps.doneDescription:
The column Latency gives the cycles that each instruction takes to execute in this processor:
memory load 4, float addition 2, integer operations and branch 1.

validation.message: Click the type button of the Program panel

steps.title: One instruction at a time
steps.questionText:
A starting point: the sequential execution model. It is the simplest possible design, and real processors do not work like this: we use it only for a moment, to compare it next with the multiple-issue, out-of-order execution of current processors.

Imagine the execution engine handles one instruction at a time:
Dispatch (1 cycle), Execute (its latency) and Write the result (1 cycle),
   and only then dispatches the next instruction.

How many cycles does one iteration of program Base take (2 loads, 2 float additions, 3 integer/branch)?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: 2 × (1+4+1) + 2 × (1+2+1) + 3 × (1+1+1) = 12 + 8 + 9 = 29 cycles. Seven times more than the 4 measured!
steps.numericWrong: Each instruction takes 1 + latency + 1 cycles, and they do not overlap: add the 7 instructions.

steps.title: Check it: the timeline
steps.description:
The Timeline of the sequential execution of the program (simplified model) shows each instruction (rows) cycle by cycle (columns), as it passes through the different instruction processing stages:
    D dispatch
    E execute (also loads and stores)
    W write the result
    R retire

One iteration takes 29 cycles.

steps.title: 6. Pipelining
steps.description:
• Pipelining divides the processing of an instruction (I1, I2, I3 …) into stages that work at the same time, each one on a different instruction (an assembly line):

• A bypass gives the result of an instruction directly to the next one that needs it.

• An instruction can start executing only when its input data are ready: a data dependence.

steps.title: The execution engine
steps.description:
To overlap many instructions, a processor has an execution engine. The instructions come from the front-end (not simulated by RVCAT) and are Dispatched in program order, both to the Waiting Buffer and to the ROB.

From the Waiting Buffer, each instruction goes to an execution port as soon as its data are ready and a port is free, and executes (E), even before older instructions that are still waiting. Its result goes to the waiting instructions by the bypass and to the ROB (W). The ROB keeps all the instructions in flight in program order, and Retires them in order, writing the registers.

steps.title: 7. Many instructions in flight
steps.description:
Now the ROB can keep many instructions in flight (100), although the processor still dispatches and retires one instruction per cycle.

Each execution port is a pipelined unit: it can start a new instruction every cycle, while the previous ones go on through its stages. Each type of instruction can use some ports, and the timeline shows the port actually used by each instruction.

steps.title: Explore the timeline
steps.description:
Drag the timeline to move it, use the mouse wheel to zoom, and hover any cell for details; hover a row's first cell to inspect that instruction.

Hover a cell where an instruction waits (.): the instructions it waits for are marked, in the timeline and in the Program panel, whose column Ports gives the ports of each type of instruction.

Click 🔍 Explore: this card is hidden and the timeline gets more room. Two new symbols appear: . and -.
steps.exploreHint: When you are done exploring, click Continue to go back to the lesson: next, there are questions on how to interpret the information of the timeline.

steps.title: Time per iteration
steps.questionText:
Find it in the timeline: how many cycles per iteration does the loop take now?

(Hint: look for a pattern that repeats in the timeline, and from it infer the average time per iteration of a loop with many iterations.)
steps.numericCorrect: Right: after the first cycles, the timeline repeats the same pattern every 7 cycles, one iteration each time (here, one instruction dispatched per cycle and 7 instructions per iteration): on average 7 cycles per iteration (7.01 in a simulation of 1,000 iterations), instead of 29.
steps.numericWrong: Look for the pattern that repeats in the timeline (the cells of one iteration, shifted to the right): how many cycles separate two repetitions? In a loop with many iterations, that is the average time per iteration (the first iterations may differ).

steps.title: The dot .
steps.questionText: In the timeline, what does a dot . mean?

answers.text: The instruction is in the execution engine, waiting for its input data (the result of a previous instruction)
answers.explanation: Yes: it waits because of a data dependence. When the result it needs is ready, it executes.

answers.text: The instruction is waiting to be dispatched
answers.explanation: No: the instruction has already been dispatched (see the D before the dots).

answers.text: The instruction is executing
answers.explanation: No: execution is E.

answers.text: The instruction has finished and waits to retire
answers.explanation: No: that is the dash -.

steps.title: The dash -
steps.questionText: And what does a dash - mean?

answers.text: The instruction has executed and written its result, and waits to retire: older instructions have not retired yet
answers.explanation: Yes: instructions retire in program order, one per cycle here.

answers.text: The instruction waits for its input data
answers.explanation: No: that is the dot.

answers.text: The instruction was cancelled
answers.explanation: No: all the instructions of this loop are useful; they wait to retire.

answers.text: The instruction executes for several cycles
answers.explanation: No: execution is shown with E, one per cycle.

steps.title: Two instructions in the same port
steps.questionText: Look at the two loads of an iteration (instructions 0 and 2): both use the same port, and their E cells overlap. How can two instructions be executing at the same time in the same port?

answers.text: The port is pipelined: it starts one instruction per cycle, and each one goes on through the next stages of the execution unit while the following one starts
answers.explanation: Yes: the two loads are in different stages of the same unit, like two cars in a car wash.

answers.text: The port can start two instructions in the same cycle
answers.explanation: No: look at the first E of each load: they start in different cycles.

answers.text: Each load uses half of the port
answers.explanation: No: each load uses the whole port, but only during one cycle in each stage.

answers.text: It is an approximation of the timeline
answers.explanation: No: the processor really works like this.

steps.title: Out-of-order execution
steps.questionText: Look at the order of the E cells. What is out-of-order execution?

answers.text: An instruction executes as soon as its input data are ready, even before older instructions that are still waiting
answers.explanation: Yes: for example, i = i + 1 and the comparison execute before the second addition of the same iteration, which waits for its data.

answers.text: Instructions are dispatched in any order
answers.explanation: No: the D cells appear in program order, one per cycle.

answers.text: Instructions retire in any order
answers.explanation: No: the R cells appear in program order.

answers.text: The compiler changes the order of the instructions
answers.explanation: No: the program is the same; the processor decides when each instruction executes.

steps.title: Dependences and bypass
steps.questionText: Which of these statements about the data dependences of Base are true? Select all the true ones.

answers.text: sum = sum + tmp needs the result of a load (tmp)
answers.explanation: Yes: each addition waits for the load of V[i] or W[i].

answers.text: sum = sum + tmp needs the result of the previous addition, also from the previous iteration
answers.explanation: Yes: the chain of sum goes across iterations.

answers.text: c = i != N needs the result of i = i + 1
answers.explanation: Yes: the comparison uses the new value of i.

answers.text: An instruction executes in the cycle after the last E of the instruction it depends on (bypass)
answers.explanation: Yes: the bypass gives it the result without waiting for W.

answers.text: An instruction waits for the W of the instruction it depends on
answers.explanation: No: look at the timeline: it executes right after the last E of its producer.

answers.text: The loads need the results of the additions
answers.explanation: No: the additions need the loads, not the other way round.

steps.title: Why dispatch and retire in order?
steps.description:
The execution engine dispatches and retires the instructions in program order, but executes them out of order. Why?

Dispatch in order. The processor takes the instructions in program order and, when it dispatches each one, connects it with the instructions that produce its input data (register renaming): inside, it builds a graph of the dependences. Then each instruction can execute as soon as its inputs are ready, out of order.

Retire in order. An instruction executed early may have to be undone (for instance after a mispredicted branch, or an exception). Its result becomes final only when it retires, in program order: if something goes wrong, the instructions after it are discarded, and the program behaves as if it were executed sequentially.

steps.title: The execution engine in detail
steps.description:
The execution engine seen before, now with the parameters of the processor of this lesson: up to 4 instructions dispatched and retired per cycle, up to 100 in flight (the ROB), and 4 pipelined execution ports, each one for some types of instruction and with their latency.

Question: with this configuration (the real one), how many cycles per iteration will the loop of Base take now? Think about it: you will check it in the next card.

steps.title: A real processor: many instructions at once
steps.description:
Back to the real configuration: up to {{dispatch}} instructions dispatched per cycle, up to {{rob}} in flight, executed out of order as soon as their data are ready (and retired in order).

Instructions of different iterations overlap (one colour per iteration).

A new symbol appears in the timeline: *. Hover over it to find out what it means.

You can click 🔍 Explore to analyse the timeline before the next questions.
steps.exploreHint: When you are done exploring, click Continue to go back to the lesson: next, questions on the time per iteration and on the meaning of *.

steps.title: Time per iteration, out of order
steps.questionText:
With up to 4 instructions dispatched per cycle, how many cycles per iteration does the loop take now?

(Look for the pattern that repeats in the timeline, and infer the average time per iteration of a loop with many iterations.)
steps.numericCorrect: Right: once the pattern repeats, a new iteration starts every 4 cycles: on average 4 cycles per iteration (4.01 in a simulation of 1,000 iterations), like the real processor. Why not less? The next cards explain it.
steps.numericWrong: Look for the pattern that repeats (one colour per iteration): how many cycles separate the start of two iterations, once the first ones have passed?

steps.title: The asterisk *
steps.questionText: In the timeline, what does an asterisk * mean?

answers.text: The instruction has its input data ready, but no port that can execute it is free in that cycle: it waits for a port
answers.explanation: Yes: a port conflict. Hovering a * shows the instruction that uses the port in that cycle.

answers.text: The instruction waits for its input data
answers.explanation: No: that is the dot.

answers.text: The instruction is executing in two ports
answers.explanation: No: an instruction uses only one port.

answers.text: The instruction has finished and waits to retire
answers.explanation: No: that is the dash -.

steps.title: A new value of i too early?
steps.questionText:
With 4 instructions dispatched per cycle, look at an iteration: i = i + 1 can execute before an older instruction of the same iteration that uses i (e.g. a load of V[i] or W[i]).

How is it possible that the older instruction still gets the previous value of i?

answers.text: At dispatch, each instruction is connected with the producer of its inputs (register renaming): the new value of i is another copy (another physical register), so the older instruction keeps the previous one
answers.explanation: Yes: renaming removes the false dependence on the name i; only the true data dependences remain.

answers.text: i = i + 1 waits until all the older instructions that use i have executed
answers.explanation: No: look at the timeline: its E can come before theirs.

answers.text: The older instruction reads i again from memory
answers.explanation: No: i is a value of the processor (a register), not a memory variable.

answers.text: The older instruction is executed again later, with the right value
answers.explanation: No: nothing is executed twice; each instruction gets the value it needs from the start.

steps.title: 8. The critical path
steps.description:
The Critical button marks in red the critical execution path, a detailed explanation of the execution time: it provides a diagnosis that may help to devise ideas to improve performance. The critical path is the chain of events, going back from the last instruction retired in the visible cycles, that links the reasons for an instruction to wait: a data dependence, a port conflict, a full ROB, a dispatch or retire width limit…

In this example, most of the cycles of the critical path come from the chain of additions to sum: sum → sum → sum…, two additions of 2 cycles per iteration: 2 + 2 = 4 cycles. Every other instruction executes for free, overlapped with this chain.

Experiment: change the number of Cycles of the timeline (e.g. 10, 20, 60) and watch how the critical path changes. A critical path of only the first few iterations can show causes (e.g. the first loads) that do not represent the performance of the loop with many iterations: look at the path once it repeats.
steps.exploreHint: When you are done exploring, click Continue to go back to the lesson: next, a question on the critical path of V1.

steps.title: Why is V1 twice as fast?
steps.questionText: V1 computes tmp = V[i] + W[i] and then sum = sum + tmp. Why does it take 2 cycles per iteration instead of 4?

answers.text: Only one addition per iteration depends on the previous iteration: the chain of sum has 2 cycles
answers.explanation: Yes: V[i] + W[i] does not depend on sum, so it overlaps with the chain.

answers.text: V1 executes fewer instructions
answers.explanation: No: V1 executes the same 7 instructions per iteration.

answers.text: The additions of V1 have a lower latency
answers.explanation: No: they are the same float additions, of 2 cycles.

answers.text: V1 uses more ports
answers.explanation: It uses the same ports; the difference is the chain of dependences.

steps.title: Experiment: a faster addition
steps.description:
Make Base run below 2.5 cycles per iteration changing only the latency of FLOAT.ADD.
In the Processor panel, click show operation types, then the FLOAT cell, and change its latency;
then simulate (Simulation panel). Predict first: what latency do you need?

steps.title: 9. Two bounds on performance
steps.description:
Static Analysis computes, without simulating, two lower bounds of the time per iteration:
• latency bound: the longest cyclic chain of dependences (sum: {{latencyBound}} cycles);
• throughput bound: the busiest resource (here port P1, with the 2 loads: {{throughputBound}}).
Minimum time = max(latency bound, throughput bound) = {{minTime}} cycles per iteration.

steps.title: In depth: the dependence graph
steps.description:
• The dependence graph shows one box per iteration and the arrows of the data dependences.
• Cyclic dependences, in red, cross iterations: they set the latency bound.
• Click a row of Latency bounds to highlight its chain (▶ Show me does it for sum).

steps.title: The bounds of V2
steps.questionText: Look at the static analysis of V2 (selected now). What is its minimum time per iteration, in cycles?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: the chain of sum has 4 additions of 2 cycles = {{latencyBound}} cycles per iteration of 2 elements: 4 cycles per element, like Base. Unrolling did not shorten the chain.
steps.numericWrong: Take the maximum of the latency bound and the throughput bound of V2.

steps.title: 10. Summary
steps.description:
• The compiler turns C into machine instructions; you can help it (options, rewriting the code).
• Time does not follow the number of instructions nor the sum of their latencies:
   a modern processor overlaps them, and the dependences set the pace.
• Minimum time = max(latency bound, throughput bound): find what limits your loop first.
All the panels of the simulator are now visible. Exit lesson returns it to its previous state.
